content: To navigate this document effectively, you can click on specific links to advance to particular topics. Additionally, hyperlinks are provided to related topics within other sections of the document. Clicking on these hyperlinks will take you to the relevant section, and you can return to the original section as needed. This summary is specifically designed for clinical providers working in healthcare facilities who serve individuals with HIV. These providers include physicians, registered nurses, advanced practice nurses, physician assistants, dentists, mental health providers, pharmacists, health educators, case managers, social workers, and counselors. Some of these professionals may also be employees or contractors of health departments. The 2014 guideline, titled Recommendations for HIV Prevention with Adults and Adolescents with HIV in the United States, includes updated and expanded federal guidance on biomedical, behavioral, and structural interventions aimed at reducing HIV transmission. These interventions focus on decreasing the infectiousness of individuals with HIV and minimizing their risk of exposing others to the virus. This guideline builds upon earlier federal guidance from 2003, which addressed incorporating HIV prevention into the medical care of individuals living with HIV. The 2014 guideline and this summary were developed collaboratively by several organizations, including the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), the National Institutes of Health (NIH), and various professional associations such as the American Academy of HIV Medicine and the Association of Nurses in AIDS Care. This summary includes recommendations related to 11 domains of interventions that can reduce HIV transmission. It provides practical strategies for implementing these recommendations, links to federal guidance supporting these interventions, and access to an online resource library with materials to aid implementation. Clinical providers can use this summary to: Learn how they and their healthcare facilities can promote HIV prevention among their patients with HIV. Select interventions that are well-suited to their patients' needs. Train staff on best practices in HIV prevention for individuals with HIV. The complete 2014 guideline is available online and is directed at professionals serving individuals or populations with HIV, including clinical providers, nonclinical providers, and staff or contractors of health departments and HIV planning groups. The context of HIV prevention involves understanding individual, social, structural, ethical, legal, and policy issues that shape the lives of individuals with HIV. Clinical providers who are aware of these issues are better equipped to foster shared responsibility and decision-making with their patients. This includes motivating patients to adopt prevention strategies, endorsing treatment as prevention to benefit community well-being, and communicating in a sensitive, respectful, and culturally competent manner. Federal, state, and local laws and policies regulate various aspects of HIV care, including the rights and responsibilities of individuals with HIV regarding disclosure of their status, unintentional or intentional exposure of others to HIV, and provider responsibilities related to case reporting, confidentiality, informed consent, and nondiscrimination. Clinical providers play a critical role in describing the benefits of early initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART), offering and prescribing ART, managing long-term ART use, and providing information on other interventions to reduce HIV transmission risk. They can also inform patients about prophylactic medications for uninfected partners to reduce their risk of acquiring HIV. Specialty services are essential for individuals with HIV who face significant personal, social, and structural challenges, such as poverty, mental illness, substance use, and unstable housing. These services can improve health outcomes, reduce HIV transmission risk, and support the use of HIV prevention and care services. Clinical providers can either offer these services onsite or refer patients to other specialty providers or agencies, ensuring follow-up to confirm access to these services. Reproductive health care is a critical component for individuals with HIV who wish to prevent unplanned pregnancies or reduce the risk of sexual HIV transmission while attempting conception. Clinical providers can offer reproductive health counseling, contraceptive services, and information on special conception methods that lower the risk of HIV transmission. Pregnant women with HIV require specialized prevention and care services to prevent transmission to their fetuses and newborns. Clinical providers can offer interventions to prevent HIV transmission during pregnancy and postpartum, as well as provide guidance on breastfeeding, which is not recommended for HIV-infected women in the United States. Sexually transmitted disease (STD) preventive services are an integral part of HIV prevention, as certain STDs can increase the risk of HIV transmission. Clinical providers should assess behavioral and biological risk factors, screen for asymptomatic STDs, provide treatment, and offer partner services. This summary also addresses quality improvement and program evaluation methods to enhance the delivery of HIV prevention and care services.
